title: Farid's successor
hookLine: tradition says Nanak met Farid's spiritual heir at Pakpattan and gathered Farid's verses

lines: A BOX OF LETTERS IN AN ATTIC.
KEEP THEM, OR LET THEM GO?
A SUFI SHRINE BY THE RIVER.
cards: A box of letters turns up in an attic after a grandparent dies. Nobody knew they existed. Someone has to decide: keep them, copy them, or let them go out with the old furniture.
Words get lost that way, one attic at a time. Sikh tradition keeps a story about a meeting where some old verses could have been lost, and weren't.
It happens in a river town in the Punjab, at the shrine of a Sufi poet who had died long before.

teach.b: We met Sheikh Farid back in year one: the Sufi of Pakpattan, whose couplets in the Granth are in Punjabi, the language of the fields. Today is about how his words traveled.
Tradition says Guru Nanak came to Pakpattan on his journeys and met the man then sitting in Farid's seat, his spiritual heir, a Sufi teacher in Farid's line.

The janamsakhis picture two seekers talking, not a contest: about God, about love, about how a person should live. In the telling, the Sufi recites Farid's verses, and Nanak listens closely enough to carry them away.

Tradition says that is how Farid's couplets came into the Guru's keeping, passed along the line of Gurus until they were written into the Granth. Historians discuss the details; the story is the one Sikhs tell.
Here is one couplet, from Ang 1378, in plain paraphrase: Farid, if you are clever and fine of mind, don't write black marks against anyone else.
Bow your head and look inside your own collar. The cleverness that would list other people's faults is sent to look at its owner instead.

teach.h: THE GURUS ANSWER FARID ON THE PAGE.
teach.b: And look at the page itself. Among Farid's couplets sit couplets by the Gurus, answering him, adding a line, gently turning a thought. A Sufi and the Gurus, side by side, in conversation.
The verses weren't just stored. They were kept alive by being talked with.

how: Sheikh Farid's couplets are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are read and sung in gurdwaras like the rest of Gurbani, and Sikhs retell the sakhi of Nanak at Pakpattan as part of how those verses came to be kept.

games.q: you're a traveler at a shrine, and a stranger recites old verses by a poet long dead. you may never pass this way again. what do you do?
o: listen closely enough to carry them away.
ask for a written copy later.
games.why: in the story, Nanak listened closely and carried Farid's verses with him; tradition says that is how they came into the Guru's keeping.

practice: Say today's couplet slowly to yourself: don't write black marks against anyone else; look inside your own collar.

Let one person you've been quietly keeping a list on come to mind, and without excusing them, set the list down for a while and look at your own collar instead. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Farid's successor. The Sufi in Farid's seat at Pakpattan who, in the story, shared Farid's verses with Nanak, so they could be kept.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a short verse or couplet; Farid's verses in the Granth are saloks.
